title: Aids to Reflection; and, The Confessions of an Inquiring Spirit
author: Samuel Taylor Coleridge
public_title: Why Your Guilt Feels Like Truth Part 3 🧠
hook: You feel guilty when you make a mistake.

sections.title: Story
sections.narration: You feel guilty when you make a mistake. Coleridge said in 1840 that this guilt is just a mirror of your own doubt. Modern science finally saw the same thing. In 1990, psychologist Paul Rozin found that people rate their own guilt about twice as high as strangers do. The result? Your brain amplifies bad feelings to keep you safe. That is not truth. It is a warning system. So why do we assume guilt means we are bad? Because the feeling is so strong. But a 2015 study by Tania Singer at the Max Planck Institute showed that guilt actually shrinks when you talk to someone. It does not grow. Coleridge was right that we are inquiring spirits. He was wrong that the pain is permanent. It is a signal, not a sentence. So next time you feel guilty, remember that it is just a signal. You feel guilty when you make a mistake.

Guilt intensity decreases significantly when individuals discuss their actions with others
